article_text:
Japanese studio giant Toho ’s North American release of “ Godzilla Minus One ” was a turning point in the company’s approach to the global market, CEO Matsuoka Hiro said at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Thursday.

Matsuoka was speaking at an “Academy in Tokyo” session with Bill Kramer, CEO of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. The film went on to gross $57.1 million in North America.

The result grew out of an opportunity Matsuoka encountered during a U.S. trip. In conversations with exhibitors, he heard that Hollywood studios were not making enough films to meet audience demand. They suggested Toho consider anime; Matsuoka said the discussions helped him recognize the popularity of Japanese animation in the U.S. Since Toho already had “Godzilla,” the company decided to take the franchise to the market itself.

The move was not an obvious one inside Toho. Matsuoka said colleagues were concerned when he proposed the U.S. release, as the company had previously struggled to distribute its films successfully outside Japan. But the film performed well, and, he said, the revenue returned to Toho.

“It was all a coincidence,” Matsuoka said of the opportunity. “It wasn’t a strategy; we just tried.”

For Matsuoka, the experience showed the value of testing new approaches as Toho expands its international business. Toho’s follow-up, Yamazaki Takashi’s “ Godzilla Minus Zero ,” will open in Japan on Nov. 3 and in North America on Nov. 6 through Gkids, the U.S. distributor Toho acquired in 2024.

The broader conversation turned to how theatrical exhibition and streaming can serve different roles in reaching audiences. Matsuoka said the two are “more like coexisting than enemies.” He noted that Japanese cinemas have drawn audiences back since the pandemic with repertory screenings, including retrospectives of Miyazaki Hayao’s films.

Kramer pointed to “Parasite” as evidence of a more global film culture, recalling director Bong Joon Ho’s remarks about audiences becoming more open to subtitles and films in other languages. Kramer also said theatrical exhibition can introduce younger generations to film history, while streaming gives films another life after their cinema run.

Asked about Asia’s share of the global film market, Kramer called the region “an extremely important market” and said it was a key reason for the Academy’s presence in Tokyo. He said 25% of the Academy’s voting members are based outside the U.S. and described partnerships with film festivals as a way to bring members together and reach potential members. The Academy’s work, he added, extends beyond the Oscars to educating people and inviting them to engage with the film industry.

The executives also addressed artificial intelligence. Matsuoka called AI a tool that could maximize workflow, while cautioning that companies should keep a close eye on its effects. Kramer said that, as the industry evolves, the Academy continues to reward human authorship and creation.

article_text:
Joel and Ethan Coen have embraced the streaming boom, working with Netflix and Apple TV+, but they remain staunch defenders of movie theaters.

Speaking at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, France on Friday, the Oscar-winning brothers were asked about their experience working with Netflix on “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs” and Apple TV+ on Joel’s “The Tragedy of Macbeth.” Joel acknowledged that changes in film distribution had also benefited independent filmmakers like themselves. In particular, the rise of home video had helped launch their careers by allowing their early films to reach wider audiences and new markets. But he was less enthusiastic about the way people are increasingly watching movies today.

“The joy of sitting in a movie theater with a crowd of people, there’s no substitute for that,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any filmmaker that enjoys the idea of working on ever diminishing platforms. ‘Oh, I saw your movie on my iPhone.’ That’s very disheartening.”

Popular on Variety

Joel Coen also praised the Lumière Film Festival for bringing large audiences together to watch films on the big screen, something he said had become increasingly difficult in the U.S.

The remarks were part of a wide-ranging masterclass hosted by festival director Thierry Frémaux, who also heads the Cannes Film Festival, ahead of the brothers receiving the festival’s lifetime achievement Lumière Award later that evening.

Despite being among the most celebrated filmmakers of their generation, the brothers were in a self-deprecating mood, sharing laughs, anecdotes and tributes to the collaborators who have helped bring their films to life.

“I always feel I am not worthy,” Ethan joked at the start of the masterclass.

The filmmakers behind “Fargo,” “The Big Lebowski” and “No Country for Old Men” spoke warmly about their four-decade partnership and their remarkably straightforward creative process.

“We’ve always written together,” Joel said. “Ethan once said the way we adapt a book is that I hold it open and he retypes it into a computer.”

“That’s why we prefer to adapt hardcover books, because of the spine,” Ethan deadpanned, drawing laughter.

Asked by Frémaux whether they ever argued, Joel described a process of bouncing ideas off each other. “Burn After Reading,” he recalled, emerged from a conversation about a movie they would never make — one opening with the typewritten words appearing: “CIA Headquarters, Langley, Virginia.”

“And then we thought, well, why don’t we make that?” he quipped.

The brothers were also keen to share credit with their longtime collaborators, repeatedly stressing that their films were the product of a collective effort.

“Us being up here, we’re taking credit for what a lot of other people have done,” Ethan said, acknowledging cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel, who was in the audience. The French DP worked with the brothers on “Inside Llewyn Davis” and “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” and with Joel on “The Tragedy of Macbeth.”

“Something emerges out of the collaboration with somebody else,” Joel said, explaining that the same principle governed his partnership with Ethan. “The secret to that kind of collaboration is knowing when the other person is right and you’re not.”

“I think we’re pretty pleasant to work with,” Ethan ventured. The reason, he joked, was that they had “very big egos” and weren’t threatened by other people’s ideas.

Frémaux turned to producer Eric Fellner, who was also in attendance, to ask whether the brothers really were so easy to work with.

“We’ve made nine films together, so I think the answer is yes,” Fellner replied. “But beyond easy, they are by far and away the most joyful people to make films with in the industry.”

Frances McDormand, Joel’s wife of more than 40 years, was also in Lyon. Joel recalled meeting the actress while casting their 1984 debut “Blood Simple,” when she was fresh out of drama school.

Thrilled with her audition, they asked her to return later that day to read with another actor. She declined, explaining that she had promised to watch her boyfriend appear on a television soap opera.

“We were like, wow, okay, that’s cool,” Joel recalled, to laughter.

The brothers also reflected on their long history with Cannes, where “Barton Fink” won the Palme d’Or in 1991. Frémaux recalled how “No Country for Old Men” left empty-handed 16 years later, despite subsequently winning four Oscars, including best picture.

Asked how they felt about missing out on prizes at Cannes, Joel recounted a Billy Wilder joke about an elderly man who complained to his doctor that he was having trouble urinating. Told the patient was 75, the doctor replied: “Well, you’ve peed enough.”

Ethan turned the punchline on their host: “Joel and I agree that your graciously having us here was your way of telling us ‘You’ve peed enough.’”

Frémaux, backed by enthusiastic cheers from the audience, assured them that the festival was eagerly awaiting their next film.

Asked which screenwriting rules they most enjoyed breaking, Ethan insisted they were barely aware of any.

Joel had some advice: “If you’re a screenwriter, you should break as many rules as you can.”

As Frémaux wrapped up the masterclass by reminding the brothers that Lyon would be celebrating them that evening, Ethan had the last word.

“We are not worthy.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: 额外的时间：在亚历山大·科贝里泽的《枯叶》中，情节退居其次，让位于运动、偶遇与离题

"格鲁吉亚电影人亚历山大·科贝里泽擅长“声东击西”的套路。在他迄今为止的三部长片中，每部都是以一个清晰可辨的叙事前提开场，随后却任由其溶解在耐心的观察之中。《让夏天永不重来》（2017）始于一个松散的成长故事，转而呈现一幅流动的第比利斯生活浮世绘；而《当我们仰望天空时看到了什么？》（2021）则以一桩灵魂互换悬案开场，进而扩展为一幅库塔伊西日常生活抒情般的画卷。情节退居其次，让位于运动、偶遇与离题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "科贝里泽的最新长片《枯叶》将这种运作方式推向了令人惊叹的极致。在一个看似失踪人口故事的开头，格鲁吉亚某体育大学的老师伊拉克利开始在乡间奔波，寻找他的女儿丽莎——一名在留下了一封模糊的信后便消失的摄影师。关于她行踪的唯一线索是她一直在进行的一个项目，即记录散布在格鲁吉亚地貌中的足球场。丽莎为什么会失踪？足球——她和父亲共同的热情——与此有什么关系吗？为了寻找答案，伊拉克利（由导演的亲生父亲大卫·科贝里泽饰演）踏上了探访一个又一个球场的旅程，希望在途中的某个地方，会有人见过她。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "接着便是“声东击西”。随着伊拉克利在村庄之间穿梭，科贝里泽非但没有加快影片的节奏，反而将其放缓，从容不迫地停留在他主人公的每一次偶遇中。农民们停下来与伊拉克利交谈，陌生人提供着记忆的碎片，孩子们指着他穿过的空间里曾经存在过的事物——那些曾经进行过比赛或举行过聚会的场地。一个男孩解释了严寒是如何摧毁葡萄园的：先是他们的生计，然后是他们的食物。一位老人邀请伊拉克利走进一个废弃的乡村俱乐部，向他展示它当年的样子，回忆起在一场地震让这里空置多年之前充满活力的过去。镜头还驻足于穿梭在这些空间中的动物——在树荫下小憩的猫，在开阔场地吃草的牛，在空旷道路上游荡的狗。伊拉克利寻找女儿的过程在长达三个小时的片长中悠长地舒展开来，变成了一场对其他消逝之物的沉思——关于生活、社区和传统的消逝。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有那些字面意义上的隐形人。我们经常看到伊拉克利与从未出现在画格中的角色交谈——比如他的旅伴莱万，他的声音是其在电影中留下的唯一痕迹。伊拉克利甚至有一两次主动伸手去和某人握手，而镜头随后却揭示那里空无一人。我们的眼睛在画格中搜寻，期望电影能恢复对话惯常的视觉逻辑。但这种情况发生得越多，就越发清晰地表明这种缺席是一种邀请：通过将某些角色置于视线之外，电影将我们的注意力从人转移到了他们所居住的空间上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "科贝里泽用一台过时的索尼爱立信手机摄像头亲自拍摄了这部电影——这也是他拍摄《让夏天永不重来》时使用的同一台设备。这部手机属于这样一个时代：数字相机突然无处不在，但它们的影像仍然感觉脆弱，容易破碎。通过将格鲁吉亚的地貌通过它进行过滤，科贝里泽将这种质感转化为了潜台词；颗粒感是一个转瞬即逝的技术时刻所留下的残余。电影在低分辨率、印象派的迷雾中展开，视觉效果如此像素化且不稳定，以至于将地貌搅动成了一片片色彩与光影的冲洗。对于习惯了超清晰数字摄影的眼睛来说，这可能会显得有些生硬，但渐渐地，这种模糊变成了一种迷恋。在某个时刻，镜头放大到一片树叶上，直到影像变得完全抽象，然后又拉回镜头，揭示我们已经移动到了一个完全不同的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种视觉瞬移正是科贝里泽式的魔幻现实主义。这位编剧兼导演利用这种过时的技术，召唤出了一种穷人电影，在影像本身中寻找弹性，让世界感觉流动、多孔且略微触不可及。与其说是虚幻事物的闯入，不如说是对我们如何看待现实的一种微妙重新定位，更接近植根于感知的魔幻现实主义传统。通过柔化世界数字化的锐利感，科贝里泽暗示奇妙并非与日常生活分离，而是已经嵌入其中。我们只需要眯起眼睛。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着影片接近尾声，寻找丽莎的过程经历了最后一次转变。在重走她摄影项目足迹的过程中，伊拉克利不再是在追逐一个幽灵；他正在占据她的视线。他所造访的足球场显现为群落建筑的最后残余——那些在周围村庄逐渐凋零时依然存在的、开辟出来的长方形土地。它们是已回归自然的仪式空间，球门柱如骨架般伫立。空旷、杂草丛生并在低分辨率的光晕中沐浴，这些球场最终不再是线索，而是变成了父女最终相遇的共享空间。由《枯叶》留给观众的并非找到失踪人员的结局，而是一个依然顽强且美丽地活着的世界那切实而持久的质感。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Georgian filmmaker Alexandre Koberidze specializes in the bait and switch. In each of his three features so far, he starts with a recognizable narrative premise only to let it dissolve into patient observation. Let the Summer Never Come Again (2017) begins as a loose coming-of-age story before giving way to a drifting portrait of life in Tbilisi, while What Do We See When We Look at the Sky? (2021) opens as a body-swap mystery before expanding into a lyrical portrait of everyday life in Kutaisi. Plot becomes secondary to movement, encounter, and digression.

Koberidze’s latest feature, Dry Leaf , takes this modus operandi to thrilling extremes. In what seems like the start of a missing-person yarn, Irakli, a teacher at a sports university in Georgia, begins traveling across the countryside searching for his daughter, Lisa, a photographer who disappeared after leaving behind a vague letter. The only clue to her whereabouts is a project she’d been working on, documenting football fields scattered across the Georgian landscape. Why did Lisa vanish? And does football, her and her father’s shared passion, have anything to do with it? In search of answers, Irakli (played by the director’s own father, David Koberidze) sets off to visit one field after another, hoping that somewhere along the way, someone might have seen her.

Then comes the bait and switch. As Irakli moves from village to village, Koberidze slows rather than quickens the pace of the film, dwelling leisurely in each of his protagonist’s encounters. Farmers pause to speak with Irakli, strangers offer fragments of memory, and children point out what once existed in the spaces he passes through—fields where games were played or gatherings took place. A boy explains how the frost took the vineyard: first their livelihood, then their food. An elderly man invites Irakli into an abandoned village club to show him what it once was, recalling a lively past before an earthquake left it empty for years. The camera also lingers on the animals that traverse these spaces—cats resting in the shade, cows grazing in open fields, dogs wandering across empty roads. Stretching languorously across the film’s three-hour runtime, Irakli’s search for his daughter becomes a reflection on other disappearances—of lives, communities, traditions.

Then there are the literally invisible people. We often see Irakli conversing with characters who never appear in the frame—like his traveling companion Levan, whose voice is his only trace in the movie. Once or twice Irakli even reaches out to shake someone’s hand, only for the camera to reveal that no one is there. Our eyes search the frame, expecting the film to restore the usual visual logic of conversation. But the more it happens, the clearer it becomes that the absence is an invitation: by keeping certain characters out of view, the film redirects our attention from people to the spaces they inhabit.

Koberidze shot the film himself on an obsolete Sony Ericsson cellphone camera—the same device that he used for Let the Summer Never Come Again . The phone belongs to an era when digital cameras were suddenly everywhere, but their images still felt fragile, prone to breaking apart. By filtering the Georgian landscape through it, Koberidze turns that texture into a subtext; the grain is the residue of an ephemeral technological moment. The film unfolds in a low-res, impressionistic haze, the visuals so pixelated and unstable that they swirl the landscape into washes of color and light. For eyes accustomed to ultra-crisp digital cinematography, it may be jarring, but gradually, the blur becomes a kind of enchantment. At one point, the camera zooms in on a patch of leaves until the image becomes completely abstract, then pulls back to reveal that we’ve moved to an entirely different place.

This visual teleportation is Koberidze’s brand of magical realism. Working with this out-of-date technology, the writer-director conjures a kind of cine pobre , finding elasticity in the image itself and making the world feel fluid, porous, and slightly out of reach. It is less an intrusion of the unreal than a subtle reorientation of how we see reality, closer to a tradition of magical realism grounded in perception. By softening the world’s digital sharpness, Koberidze suggests that the marvelous is not separate from the everyday, but already embedded within it. We just have to squint.

Sound becomes the film’s most stable reality. When Irakli speaks to Levan, we hear the rustle of fabric, the shift of weight on gravel. These details give concrete presence to what isn’t visible. The film treats the invisible as already there, registering beyond the visual, through sound and other forms of perception. The soundscape is primarily environmental—wind, bells, animals—and these noises function not as background, but as equal participants in the story. Giorgi Koberidze’s score begins with a staccato, syncopated rhythm that feels separate from the scenery, before it yields to the ambient space, allowing the hum of the countryside to take over.

As the film approaches its end, the search for Lisa undergoes a final transformation. In retracing the path of her photography project, Irakli is no longer chasing a ghost; he is occupying her gaze. The football fields he visits emerge as the last vestiges of communal architecture—rectangles of cleared earth that persist even as the villages around them thin out. They are spaces of ritual that have reverted to nature, goalposts standing like skeletal remains. Empty, overgrown, and bathed in that low-res glow, the fields eventually cease to be clues and instead become shared spaces where father and daughter finally meet. Dry Leaf leaves the viewer not with the closure of a missing person found, but with the tangible and enduring texture of a world that remains, stubbornly and beautifully, alive.

article_text:
Great documentaries never turn out quite the way you plan them. You might start out thinking that you’re making one film , but a documentarian has to be willing to accept when changes in the lives of their subjects changes the nature of their project.

Julia Loktev ‘s two-part documentary “ My Undesirable Friends ” is a perfect example of this. The films, which follow journalists at TV Rain, which was Russia’s last independent news channel before it was shut down over coverage of the war in Ukraine, began as a story about journalists working in a hostile climate. But when her subjects were forced to flee the country and scatter across Europe, “My Undesirable Friends” had to expand its scale.

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event, Loktev opened up about the project’s origins. While she had already been shooting footage of her subjects, the films truly took shape the week Russia invaded Ukraine.

“Neither of these two films were supposed to happen,” Loktev said. “I just started making a film that I thought was gonna be called ‘The Lives of Foreign Agents’ about these young journalists that were being called foreign agents. And the media were being called undesirable organizations. Of course, what we didn’t know was that four and a half months later, Russia would start a full scale war with Ukraine and shut down all independent media within that first week.”

“‘Part II’ starts right after all these journalists were forced to leave the country,” she continued. “Putin calls them the flies that Russia spits out of its mouth. But that first week was terrifying. Nobody could imagine invading Ukraine. The war had been going for eight years, but it was the kind of year where the world allowed Russia to host a world cup… All of these journalists tried to report the truth to Russians, and up until that moment they were living in Russia. Maybe you were waiting for the police to show up at your office or your home, maybe friends of yours were being arrested, but you could still work in Russia. And then that stopped.”

Watch the complete conversation with Loktev in the video above.

Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com , or find us on Facebook , Twitter , Instagram , and YouTube .

article_text:
Das wichtigste Festival des fantastischen Films außerhalb der USA öffnet am 8. Oktober an Spaniens Mittelmeerküste seine Pforten und die Prominenz aus Hollywood steht Schlange. Bis zum 18. Oktober laufen in dem kleinen Ort in Katalonien internationale Neuentdeckungen aus dem Bereich des Unheimlichen, Monströsen und Magischen.

Nachdem vor einem Jahr der Independent-Film „ Obsession “ seine Europa-Premiere im 30.000-Seelennest Sitges nahe Barcelona feierte und dort gleich drei Preise samt Publikumspreis einheimste, war jedem Verleiher klar, dass man im neben dem „ Fantastic Fest “ in Austin und dem „ Fantasia International “ in Montreal wichtigsten Festival des fantastischen Films der Welt auch auf Perlen fürs breite Publikum stoßen kann. Das aufs Unheimliche spezialisierte Festival, das dieses Jahr bereits zum 59. Mal stattfindet, hat sich übers Nischenpublikum hinaus zur wichtigen Plattform entwickelt. Nicht nur Abseitiges in Sachen Grenzüberschreitungen wartet hier auf abgehärtete Horrorfans, sondern auch Animiertes und Dokumentarisches; Gewitztes und sogar für Kinder Goutierbares gibt es beim Sitges Film Festival vor und nach der Geisterstunde zu bestaunen.

Das Sitges Filmfestival 2025

Warum "Obsession" sämtliche Rekorde bricht

Die Stars der Branche lieben das kleine Genrefestival am Mittelmeer südlichwestlich von Cannes, das im Gegensatz zur Festival-Maschine an der Cote d’Azur noch sehr geerdet und familiär daherkommt. Das zeigt sich nicht nur am „Zombie-Wochenende“, wenn sich alle wie sonst nur zu Karneval schminken lassen und durch die engen Gassen der Altstadt schlurfen oder den lauen Herbstmond anheulen dürfen. Unter anderem Peter Jackson , Robert Eggers , Rick Baker und Danny DeVito haben sich aus den USA und Takashi Shimizu und Na Hong-Jin aus Asien angesagt. Wichtiger als die Weltstars sind jedoch die kommenden Film-Entdeckungen. Im Wettbewerb des Festivals treten unter anderem der australische Coming-of-Age-Horror „ Leviticus “, die britische Folkhorror-Komödie „ The Incomer “, der US-Survival-Thriller „ The River “ und der südkoreanische Zombiefilm „ Colony “ gegeneinander an; zahlreiche weitere Überraschungen warten in den Nebensektionen, unter anderem den auf Experimentelles und Ungewöhnliches spezialisierten „Noves Visiones“, der kindertauglichen „Sitges Family“-Reihe oder der in Zusammenarbeit mit der katalanischen Filmkritiker-Vereinigung kuratierten Reihe „Seven Chances“. Elf Tage und ein paar hundert Filme sind Zeit dafür. Wie in Sitges üblich, buchstäblich rund um die Uhr.

Our editors on the exhibitions they’re looking forward to around the world this month – from Lagos and London to Doha and Dubai

Lagos

Lagos Biennial 2026: The Museum of Things Unseen

The latest edition of the Lagos Biennial, cocurated by New York-based artist Furen Dai, Nairobi-and-Cologne-based artist Sam Hopkins and Nigerian curator Chinyere Obieze, presents itself with no small task. Its curatorial blurb asks, ‘If we were to build a museum from scratch, unbounded by structural inequalities, what form would it take?’ The response seems to be looking both to the past – taking the biennial as occasion to launch a permanent pavilion to house the Àkéte Collection, made up of works from the biennial’s four editions since starting in 2017 (alongside international ‘donations and loans’) and a (extremely limited run) publication documenting that history – and to the future, with the main exhibition featuring contributions from 18 artists and collectives, including Ade Adekola, Olukemi Lijadu, Aki Sasamoto , Amie Siegel, Hito Steyerl and Kara Walker , responsible for providing possible further responses to such a question. That such speculation takes place within Eko Atlantic City, an area of newer ‘sustainable’ structures built on a peninsula of land, reclaimed over the past decade, that juts into the Gulf of Guinea, only further frames and complicates the responses that might be offered. Chris Fite-Wassilak

Various venues, 14 November – 6 December

London

Nan Goldin: You Never Did Anything Wrong

For the better part of five decades, photographer Nan Goldin has borne witness to the concurrent plights and pleasures of communities living outside society’s strictures of ‘normality’. In this exhibition, however, which shares its title with Goldin’s 2024 show at Gagosian New York, a series of new and recent films mark a decisive shift in the artist’s focus towards abstraction and the natural world. Alongside the brutal Memory Lost (2019–21), documenting Goldin’s own experiences of addiction , the exhibition includes You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024) and Part II (2026), which meditate on ‘animal consciousness’ and extinction, and Stendhal Syndrome (2024), juxtaposing images of Goldin’s friends and lovers with contrived art-historical references. The question is: can Goldin make these disparate references cohere into something as affecting as the lives she usually turns her camera towards? Erin-Atlanta Argun

Hayward Gallery, 24 November – 14 March

Tokyo

The Constitution of JAPAN 2026

For the past three years, the galleries AOYAMA | MEGURO and MUJIN-TO Production have presented exhibitions organised under the same premise as the book The Constitution of Japan (2019), edited by legendary art director Gento Matsumoto, which pairs each article of Japan’s legal constitution with a Japanese contemporary artwork. Opening around the anniversary of the constitution’s promulgation, in 1946, The Constitution of Japan 2026 is guest-curated by Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono. Unlike the book on which it is based, the show will feature work by artists from overseas – such as the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. With the ruling LDP and hawkish PM Sanae Takaichi pushing to revise the constitution – particularly its most radically passive Article 9 renouncing war and prohibiting possession of a military – and adopting anti-immigrant rhetoric to appease an increasingly conservative public, the exhibition couldn’t be timelier. Taro Nettleton

Aoyama Meguro and Mujinto Production, 4–29 November

Doha

Rubaiya Qatar: Unruly Waters

In Sunil Amrith’s 2018 book, Unruly Waters , the Yale professor tells the history of (predominantly southern) Asia through that primary element and its infrastructures: seas, coasts, rains and rivers, but also dams and pipelines, canals; and so too mapmakers, climatologists, infrastructural authorities and farmers. It’s a story of control, above all, as if nature’s hydrological cycle – and the lives of subaltern communities – could be mastered by plumbing as much as by violence. The inaugural Rubaiya Qatar quadrennial’s headline exhibition, curated by Tom Eccles, Ruba Katrib, Shabbir Hussain Mustafa and ArtReview ’s own Mark Rappolt, takes its title from Amrith’s book – and will look to explore the relationship between water and humanity now and in history, as well as, according to the curators, attempt to ‘redefine “globalism” through ecology and human movement, understanding it as a product of nature as much as of commerce’. (As this year’s Busan Biennale did in addressing Busan’s port beyond the gallery walls – one of the world’s busiest ports; and as did the outstanding travelling exhibition Indigo Waves and Other Stories (Zeitz MOCAA, Cape Town, 2023, and SAVVY Contemporary and Gropius Bau, Berlin, 2024) with its focus on the Afrasian Sea.) Look at contemporary art go, hot on the heels of geopolitics ! Over 30 new commissions will come from artists including Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Sophia Al-Maria, Naeem Mohaiemen, Yuko Mohri, Marina Tabassum and more . Further reading, I’d venture, includes Sabrina Mahfouz’s These Bodies of Water (2022), which pertains explicitly to the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, and Laleh Khalili’s The Corporeal Life of Seafaring (2024), taking the cargo worker as embodiment of a global economic disorder. And of course Spivak, duh! Alexander Leissle

Various venues, 21 November – 30 April

Dubai

Salah Elmur: Just as the Heart of a Mango is a Stone

In addition to brushes and acrylics, the painter Salah Elmur’s raw materials include photographs he collected from his father’s commercial portrait studio in his native Sudan: the piercing gazes of posing customers amid the noise and bustle of the nearby fish market. Elmur’s figurative abstractions – which tend to distort the proportions of his subjects and often transform scenes of daily life and local ritual into surreal vignettes – hold together this exhibition spanning three chapters of his practice. Alongside archival photographs, sketches and ephemera, we’ll see Elmur’s precursors and procedures, including its resonances with the visual vocabulary of the Khartoum School – a pioneering Modernist art movement in Africa. Elmur, who fled Khartoum, his hometown, during the 1990s (his cartoon depicting Omar al-Bashir’s 1989 coup d’état didn’t go down well), now lives in Cairo. While rarely overtly political, his tenderly executed portraits and enigmatic landscapes of memory nonetheless channel the resilience of a country long beset by political upheaval and civil war. And stand as proof that distance often yields fresh perspective. Max Crosbie-Jones

Jameel Arts Centre, through 14 March

Melbourne

Passage: The Art of Atong Atem

Drawing on traditions of African studio photography, the Melbourne-based South Sudanese artist Atong Atem uses portraiture to question how identities are constructed and performed. Faces are painted in startling shades of green, blue and violet; figures dressed in elaborate costumes pose against richly coloured backdrops; the familiar conventions of studio portraiture give way to something stranger, more theatrical. The most comprehensive survey of her work to date brings together more than 65 works created over the past decade, including new commissions. Among them is Surat (2022), in which Atem recreates photographs of relatives she knows only through old family photographs, inserting herself into histories she never lived or witnessed. Scars and Constellations (2024) connects Dinka Bor traditions of scarification and healing with colonial histories of maritime trade and navigation. A new largescale installation, As Above (2026), meanwhile, draws on Dinka dance, traditional beading and Catholic iconography to explore how different cultures have made sense of the stars. Here, it’s not so much about history being inherited, but continually reimagined. Fi Churchman

NGV Melbourne, through 14 June

New York

Beatriz Zamora: The Lost Works

When Beatriz Zamora won the Salón Nacional de Artes Plásticas prize in 1978 with her monochromatic painting El negro no. 4 – at a time when, in her words, even Pierre Soulages ‘ todavía no llegaba al negro absoluto [had not yet arrived at absolute black]’ – a disgruntled young member of the Mexican art collective Peyote y la Compañía allegedly struck the work with a fire extinguisher before grabbing and hurling it down the stairs of the Palacio de Bellas Artes. The attack was a symptom of the aggression that Zamora faced for her oft-misunderstood all-black abstractions, of which the nonagenarian has since produced over 4,000 examples using ground coal, graphite, obsidian, soot and more. It also more than justified her relocation, in 1980, from Mexico City to New York. That latter leg of her biography ended with another curious incident involving her artistic property, this time resulting incidentally in its preservation: when Zamora was denied reentry to the US in 1988, her studio assistant went rogue, disappearing with a trove of her paintings. These works, since recovered from a townhouse in Brooklyn following the assistant’s death, form a solo exhibition at Management that reckons with the time and recognition that this artist and many like her have lost to forces – and people – beyond anyone’s control. Jenny Wu

Management, 6 November – 20 December

artport: A History of Internet Art

The internet has often been declared dead, overrun by corporate entities and AI bots. So now it’s getting a retrospective. The Whitney’s artport, one of the first institutional browser-based galleries, was founded in 2001: the same year as Wikipedia, just over a decade into the existence of the World Wide Web, and at the tail end of the dotcom crash. In November it will spill into the museum’s physical galleries to showcase a quarter-century of internet art. Consider JODI’s computer program manipulations, Mendi + Keith Obadike’s online performances, Morehshin Allahyari’s hyperlink poetry or Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s investigations of AI training data. Through over 100 works commissioned for artport since its inception, the exhibition will show how artists have continuously engaged with the web as a place and a medium – and in the process recorded how the internet itself shapeshifted from its read-only beginning to slopification into oblivion. Mia Stern

Whitney Museum of American Art, 21 November – ongoing

Mérida

Bienal de Yucatán: VOCAL

Since 2007 artist Abraham Cruzvillegas has been making work under the title autoconstrucción , work that has taken myriad guises, from small sculptures and architectural installations to musical performances and theatre productions, but united in their tentative finality and a belief that all things should evolve and change through context and locale. Call it a belief in growth and empathy, or something like that. The Mexican artist says the ad hoc housing he grew up in is a foundational reference for this approach, but it is not architecture that forms the theme of the Bienal de Yucatán, the inaugural edition of which he’ll curate, but language – the verbal, the evolving tongue, the idiomatic. His show promises 76 artists, linguists, filmmakers, poets, musicians and dancers, whose work will occupy a former sixteenth-century convent and other venues in Mérida, the capital of the peninsular state. After all, there’s nothing more tentative and subject to change than one’s own voice. Oliver Basciano

Various venues, 26 November – 28 February

Berlin

Sophie Calle: Is It Better?

In The Disappearing Act (2026, translated from the original Russian, 2024), Maria Stepanova’s latest autofictional novel to explore the shame and loneliness of being in exile (‘while her home country wages war on a neighbouring state’), her heroine, M, is inspired by a ‘French artist who made an art of stalking… passersby’. So inspired that she embarks on her own game of tailing a stranger – ‘in exactly the same manner as the French artist, unburdened by guilt, shame, awkwardness, uncertainty, and all other such baggage’. Much indeed like Sophie Calle and her Suite Vénitienne (1979–80), for which she followed and took pictures of a man over multiple days in Venice, documenting her pursuit of an unknown subject. Forty-six years on, Calle’s practice – often stemming from such acts of arbitrary and at times voyeuristic investigation – still speaks to contemporary understandings of surveillance, privacy and the ways in which we relate to one another. Her fifth solo exhibition this year, Is It Better? at Hamburger Bahnhof will present six bodies of work from the past three decades – from The Detachment series (1996) to Les fantômes d’Orsay (2022) – alongside a new work, which after the show will be donated to Hamburger Bahnhof’s collection. article_text:
An alleged member of the four-person team that broke into the Louvre last October, stealing crown jewels worth roughly $100 million, has been denied release, Le Figaro reports. The suspect, Rachid H., 40, has been detained since November 2025, and will remain in pre-trial detention, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled Wednesday.

On the morning of Sunday, October 19, 2025, the gang used a truck-mounted motorized ladder to break into the Louvre’s Apollo Gallery through a second-floor window. Once inside, they smashed two display cases and grabbed eight pieces of jewelry. (A crown once owned by Empress Eugénie was dropped in their haste.) As alarms sounded, they fled and escaped on two motorized scooters. The entire heist unfolded in roughly seven minutes.

The stolen jewels have yet to be recovered, but police have made relatively more in identifying the thieves. The first two suspects were arrested within a month of the heist: Abdoulaye N., 40, an unlicensed taxi driver with prior robbery convictions who is known online for his motocross stunts, and Ghelamallah A., 36, an unemployed Algerian national. Both have admitted involvement, though their testimony has raised more questions than it has answered.

In June, the two told investigators that a sponsor, whom they declined to name, had recruited them for the heist. They claimed to have been brought on just days before October 19, and the principal accomplice who gave them the orders, they said, remains at large, while the men arrested after them—including Rachid H.—had nothing to do with the crime. The purported mastermind, they claimed, had entered the Louvre with the robbers and remains at large.

Rachid H. was detained on suspicion of having provided the robbers with the keys to the parking facility in Aubervilliers. In January, AFP reported that he admitted to having “passed” the keys to “two people” but maintained that he knew nothing about the robbery. His defense has pointed out that his client’s fingerprints were found neither on the truck used in the heist nor in the parking lot where the robbers allegedly handed the jewels to an unidentified individual.

Issue

Leaks and Losses

In late September, Victoria’s anti-corruption commission announced that a former senior executive at Melbourne’s National Gallery of Victoria had allegedly stolen approximately AUD 8 million (USD 5.6 million) from the institution over six years. The official, identified as the gallery’s former head of IT, is accused of using his authority to conceal a scheme involving hundreds of falsified documents and the purchase and resale of smartphones for personal profit. He has been charged with eight offenses, including seven counts of theft and one of misconduct in public office. The case has raised questions about how a multimillion-dollar scheme could have remained undetected for so long.

If, for whatever reason, you want to feel a bit sad, think too hard about what Elliott from ET would have been like as an adult. Or Coraline, or Matilda, or Chihiro, or those kids in Mary Poppins. The most amazing thing that ever happened in their lives – magic nanny, alien friend, psychic abilities, otherworldly adventures – was already over when they were kids. If that bad Harry Potter play taught us anything, they probably all grew into loser adults.

This is the central premise for Allen, a new Netflix family film by Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, the Brisbane production company behind a little show called Bluey. As a kid growing up in the small Sunshine Coast town of Coolum Beach, Petey (TJ Power) happens across a friendly, bug-eyed extraterrestrial; the little guy can’t quite pronounce “alien”, so they settle on “Allen”. Petey and Allen are best pals for one blissful month, sharing a love for Cheezels, VHS and board games – until suddenly, Allen is summoned home. Decades later, Petey is trapped in a state of arrested development and obsession that frustrates everyone around him – until Allen returns, for surprising reasons I will not spoil here.

There are a lot of nods to ET in Allen (“pretty aggressive nods,” Pearson laughs) – obviously the premise but also the score and even the poster, which features Allen and Petey’s fingers reaching to one another, and a floating Cheezel in the middle.

When I tell him that ET is among my favourite films, the 42-year-old winces. “Oh, no,” he says, rubbing his chin. “OK, we’ll talk about that.”

Allen, which Pearson co-directed with Jeffrey Walker and co-wrote with Sophie Miller, is the stuff of his childhood: ET, the Nightmare board game, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Lion King, Terminator 2; the opening scene tracks through Petey’s tapes, games and figurines. “I was using the stuff that I love to tell the story of not being able to let go of the stuff you love, and how it maybe holds you back,” Pearson says. So, a film about the dangers of nostalgia absolutely packed with nostalgia. Pop culture in the 1980s and 1990s was like an “onslaught”: “It was the best thing you could ever want as a child. We were like drug addicts and these corporations had us hooked.”

But just as Petey loses Allen, Pearson experienced a life-changing loss. When he was 13, his older brother Liam died of cancer aged just 26. Pearson has not talked about this much in the past, even in his personal life, but making Allen has helped him unpick how it affected him. “My family must be like, ‘Wow, he’s spoken more about this to the Courier Mail than to us!’” he laughs.

Liam’s death is intrinsically tied to why Pearson is fixated on pop culture from that point in his life. “He was my best friend, the best thing ever to me,” he says. “As much as I say Allen is about Liam, it’s sort of about the perfume of Liam – that feeling of losing something and wanting it back so badly that you don’t do anything with your life, you just sit there and wait. I only listen to old songs, I have all the old toys around the Ludo office and I only watch old movies. It connects me to a past that doesn’t exist any more. And it’s bad. And I started thinking: I’m rushing back to the womb, I’m trying to stay in that bubble that got popped.”

As well as producing the biggest kids’ show in the world, Pearson is behind another huge hit: the 2022 horror film Talk To Me . Ludo was too busy with Bluey to develop Talk To Me, so Pearson gave the concept to the Philippou brothers , who directed it. When I point out that it is another story about not being able to let go, Pearson looks stunned. “Yeah, that’s right,” he says. “I didn’t even think of that. How funny. I guess you are what you are what you are.”

This may all make Allen sound far more grave than it is – kids who don’t notice any of this will simply enjoy, as Pearson puts it, “a silly, stupid alien pulling the carpet out from people constantly”.

“We hope that bit is there for them – and for Mum and Dad, maybe some of the other bit. But not at the expense of a ridiculous alien who sings karaoke,” he says. “I hope you press play and you have a giddy time.”

The karaoke-singing alien himself required years of “intensive” development, says Pearson: “People would have invented six new Boeing planes in the time we created Allen.” Ludo and the Brisbane FX company Formation Effects initially tried to make Allen as an animatronic puppet, but the end result was “frightening”, Pearson snorts. “We’ll save that for the bad sequel where there are terrible versions of Allen.”

The final Allen is a puppet, with some VFX on top for his expressions and movement. Pearson didn’t want Allen to be “Jar Jar Binks-y or Gremlin-y – he wasn’t throwing records across the room or doing Abbott and Costello physical comedy – he’s introspective, not zany.” This meant that until his little facial expressions and monosyllabic voice were added in, Allen looked “really boring” for a long time. “The edit was a big trust process!”

The other reason Allen took so long? “It has never felt like you could put Bluey on pause. I didn’t feel confident enough that people would wait … Maybe it’s just to do with being from Queensland or Australia, but I don’t feel like those amazing production companies in America that can line up opportunities like planes.”

Wait, I say – doesn’t a success like Bluey not instill you with enough confidence to pass on one opportunity and know another will come? “I don’t feel it, if it does,” Pearson replies. “Bluey has been the luckiest thing in the world. I’m not being naive or self-effacing. I’m aware of how one-in-a-million the opportunity was and how hard everyone worked on it. But I still feel like everything could go tomorrow. Bluey just put a bit more pressure on us, I guess, because now we’re known as the people who did that!”

Allen is on Netflix from 12 November
